extracted.intended_audience: Data controllers, litigators, in-house counsel, and courts handling cross-border preservation, disclosure, and discovery of personal data
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preserving, disclosing, and discovering Protected Data in cross-border litigation, balancing U.S. discovery obligations with foreign Data Protection Laws and recommending procedures (stipulations, orders, protocols) to minimize conflicts and protect Data Subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit preservation, disclosure, and discovery to relevant and necessary data
rubrics_metrics.description: Preservation, disclosure, and discovery of Protected Data should be limited in scope to that which is relevant and necessary to support any party’s claim or defense in order to minimize conflicts of law and impact on the Data Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle recognizes obligations of Data Controller, requesting party, and court to protect Data Subjects; parties and courts should cooperate, use stipulations or court orders, and avoid producing Protected Data beyond what is relevant and necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply heightened scrutiny when Protected Data is implicated
rubrics_metrics.description: A greater degree of scrutiny is necessary to protect the rights of the Data Subject and to minimize conflicts with Data Protection Laws when Protected Data is at issue, including at early disclosure, preservation, and discovery stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If questionable whether Protected Data should be disclosed, the Data Controller should seek interim protection (stipulation or court order) until conclusively determined; do not produce Protected Data clearly outside disclosure scope even if strategically advantageous; produce data that must be disclosed only after appropriate measures (restrict distribution, confidentiality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform discovery scope to Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1) relevance and proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery obligation under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1) extends only to information that is relevant to claims and defenses and proportional to the needs of the case; apply proportionality factors when weighing discovery of Protected Data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider six proportionality factors: importance of issues at stake, amount in controversy, parties' relative access to information, parties' resources, importance of discovery in resolving issues, and whether burden/expense outweighs likely benefit. Courts may require information to be 'necessary', 'vital', or at least 'relevant' when foreign Data Protection Laws are implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the scope of requests through specificity and custodian restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties should work together to limit preservation, processing, and production to what is relevant and necessary; narrow document requests and limit custodians to fewer, more relevant individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use requests with greater specificity per Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(1); restrict breadth to fewer custodians and allow iterative extensions; courts should endorse narrowing broad requests when parties fail to reach consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid broad 'any and all' requests; use narrowly tailored requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalized, catch-all requests (e.g., 'any and all') are inappropriate and may contravene Data Protection Laws; narrow requests that clarify particular documents requested better comport with data protection principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially important in state courts that have not conformed to Federal Rules; many courts require materials implicating foreign Data Protection Laws to be not just relevant but necessary or vital to litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use phased (sequenced) discovery to minimize Protected Data exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure disclosure and production around key players initially and phase discovery to minimize volume and breadth of Protected Data while preserving ability to pursue additional data later if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a scheduling order to sequence discovery and allow time to 'legitimize' processing/transfers. Suggested chronological phasing: (1) data from U.S. sources probably not subject to Data Protection Laws; (2) as necessary, data from U.S. sources potentially subject; (3) data from foreign sources probably not subject; (4) as necessary, foreign sources potentially subject. Phasing must be proposed in good faith and not to improperly delay discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize production by filtering, anonymization, and early culling
rubrics_metrics.description: Take steps to filter data, substitute alternatives, and limit production format to reduce conflicts of law and impact on Data Subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filtering techniques include use of targeted search terms, date ranges, data-source limits, deduplication, and algorithms; filtering is best undertaken early and, where applicable, performed in the country where the data resides (Article 29 WP prefers EU-local filtering). Consider anonymization/pseudonymization where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute alternative data sources/elements when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where substitution can be done without inappropriately compromising functionality and evidentiary value, rely on alternative sources or data elements to minimize disclosure of Protected Data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitution may reduce impact on Data Subjects while still conveying adequate responsive information; must assess evidentiary sufficiency before substituting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit production format to protect Protected Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose production formats that minimize disclosure of Protected Data (for example, image format with text-searchable load file rather than native format).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format choices can shield irrelevant metadata and reduce redaction problems; consider redactions, hard-copy production, or non-native formats when appropriate to eliminate exposure of protected personal information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stipulations or court orders (protective orders) when conflicts exist
rubrics_metrics.description: When conflicts exist between Data Protection Laws and preservation/discovery obligations, parties should employ stipulations or seek court orders to protect Protected Data and minimize conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are encouraged to draft stipulations (ideally as stipulated court orders) allocating duties to protect and dispose of Protected Data consistent with applicable Data Protection Laws; if parties cannot agree, the responding party should seek a protective order. Protective orders may be negotiated or unilaterally submitted to the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate or obtain scheduling stipulation/order to allow legitimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use scheduling stipulations or court orders to set deadlines and sequencing for discovery, ensuring sufficient time to legitimize processing and transfers of Protected Data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduling orders should permit identification, collection, processing, and production of information not subject to Data Protection Laws first, thereby minimizing need for cross-border transfers; consider different timetables for each applicable Data Protection Law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a legitimization plan tailored to applicable Data Protection Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The responding party should prepare a plan describing how it will preserve, process, transfer, and produce Protected Data in a manner tailored to each applicable Data Protection Law while complying with U.S. obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimization plan may be prepared unilaterally or with requesting party/data protection authorities; the plan helps demonstrate compliance and resolves processing/transfer concerns in advance; use the Sedona Conference Protocol and Cross-Border Data Safeguarding Process + Transfer Protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare documentation demonstrating data-protection safeguards (Protocol documentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data Controllers should document that data protection obligations have been addressed and appropriate safeguards instituted, following the Sedona Conference Protocol; documentation may accompany Protected Data transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended documentation items include: (1) purpose for collection/transfer and description of matter; (2) identification/significance of Data Protection Laws and data locations; (3) measures taken to narrow/cull processing/transfers (questionnaires, iterative search, deduplication); (4) categories of Protected Data collected; (5) confirmation of protective order/stipulation (attach copy); (6) description of processes/transfers and any Data Subject notice; (7) steps to secure data prior to transfer (third-party agreements, encryption, access limits); (8) compliance with notification obligations to oversight bodies; (9) legal basis for transfer to U.S. and protective measures imposed on requesting party; (10) disposition plan when data no longer needed; (11) identification/signature of person(s) responsible and attestation that steps were taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain Protected Data only as long as necessary; preserve while litigation pending or reasonably anticipated
rubrics_metrics.description: Data Controllers should retain Protected Data only to satisfy legal or business needs; while legal action is pending or reasonably anticipated, preserve relevant information (including Protected Data) with appropriate safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage reasonable, systematic records-management and data-minimization; apply privacy-by-design to systems; preservation obligation limited in duration to pending or reasonably anticipated litigation (reasonable anticipation arises when organization is on notice of a credible probability or takes specific actions to commence litigation). Preserve reliability, integrity, confidentiality, and security while data is held. Do not use retention policies to evade preservation duties; apply uniformly and in good faith.
